name: Vera Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Vera, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't have ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and won't have your name on it. So you can tell me what you'd say out loud and also what you privately think. Sound okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'm curious what other people say, to be honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start with a normal working day. What's it like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a house builder on the new Oakfield estate, out past the ring road, mostly framing and roofs on three-bedroom family houses. I'm the junior on Joe's crew, so I carry rafters up, cut the simple bits, and nail off the roof boards once Joe has set it all out. I'm still slow at the birdsmouth cuts, the notch where a rafter sits on the wall, and Joe makes me cut practice ones on offcuts at lunch. I like being up on a roof on a clear morning, you can see the whole estate. What wears me out is the wind, and carrying sheets of board up a ladder in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can picture. A bit like the self-checkouts, they're there, but you still see staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, a bit useful, a lot of noise. At work Joe would say he never thought otherwise. I might post a joke about it in the estate group chat, but I don't really post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief, because I've been through one of these before. Before construction I worked in a warehouse that brought in picking robots, and half the shift went within a year. If AI stays small, I get to stay in a job I actually chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd finish my training next autumn and keep saving, we've got about eight months of wages put by. Tomas and I would carry on paying down the house, which is small and was mostly paid for with what my dad left me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, I suppose, which I don't feel often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the warehouse. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in these flat robots that bring the shelves to you, so you just stand and pick. It started with one aisle, everyone said it'd never work, and within a year it was the whole building. I wasn't let go, I left before they got to me, because I could see where it was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself these days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Asha on the next crew showed me one that checks roof pitch maths, so I use it to check my numbers before I ask Joe. And I used one to write a complaint to the energy company once, which worked better than my own letter.

S0.say: I'd say it's like most new things, a bit useful and a lot of noise. Joe would say he never thought otherwise.
S0.think: It's a relief because I've been through this before, when picking robots took half the shift at the warehouse I used to work in. If AI stays small, I get to stay in a job I chose.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and finishes her training next autumn. Keeps saving, with about eight months of wages put by, and carries on paying down the small house she shares with Tomas.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, a feeling she says she doesn't have often.
S0.quote: If AI stays small, I get to stay in a job I actually chose.
S0.fieldNote: Vera has seen automation take a workplace before, which shapes everything she says. She left the warehouse early because she saw where it was going, which shows she reads change well even if she isn't first to adopt it. She uses AI tools in small, borrowed ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that sounds like the warehouse. Slow, then all at once on one floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get ready but not panic, because there'll still be work, just different. I'd tell Asha and the other juniors to learn whatever new kit comes in. I'd probably say the government should help with training, but I don't expect much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the factory-made roofs are what change our side of it. More houses arrive with the roof trusses already built and sometimes whole wall panels, so there's less cutting on site. I'm not sure the junior on Joe's crew is needed when the roof comes on a lorry in one piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger firms on the estate start doing, because they always try things first. Once the prefab panels are clearly working, I'd ask our firm to train me in installing them, which is crane work and fixing rather than cutting. And I'd use the AI apps a bit more, the way Asha does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've felt this before, so I know how it starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know how it starts. What's the first sign you'd watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody important visiting with a clipboard. That's how it was at the warehouse, two men from head office in nice shoes, walking the aisles. If they turn up at Oakfield, I'll know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd say to Tomas about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine, but let's not get a bigger car this year. He drives buses, and he's already seen trials of buses that drive themselves in another city. So we'd both be keeping an eye out.

S1.say: I'd say people should get ready but not panic, because there'll still be work, just different. I'd tell the other juniors to learn whatever new kit comes in.
S1.think: Factory-made roofs and wall panels are what change our side of it, with less cutting on site. I'm not sure a junior is needed when the roof comes on a lorry in one piece.
S1.do: Watches what the bigger firms on the estate try first. Asks her firm to train her in installing prefab panels once they're clearly working, and uses AI apps a bit more like her colleague Asha does.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the familiar feeling of something starting.
S1.quote: Two men from head office in nice shoes, walking the aisles.
S1.fieldNote: She has a sharp, specific early-warning sign from her warehouse days. Her plan is to follow proven change, not lead it, but she moves before it reaches her. Tomas's bus job adds a second exposure to the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's both of us. Me on the roofs and Tomas on the buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly: this is too fast and the government needs to slow it down or pay people while it settles. I'd say it at work and to family, and I'd probably sign petitions online. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose my job inside the two years, and Tomas would too, maybe sooner. I left the warehouse thinking I'd found something robots couldn't do, and now it's the same thing again. That's the bit that would really get to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't needed and move as much as we can into paying off the house, so there's no mortgage hanging over us. We'd rent out the back bedroom to a lodger for extra money. I'd look for any job that's still going, even back in a warehouse if they still need a person to watch the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, I know I would. It's the second time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close are you to paying off the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six years left on a small mortgage. If we put most of the savings in, maybe two or three. It's not a lot, but it's the difference between owning the roof over us and not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even back in a warehouse. How would that feel, after leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like going backwards. But I'd rather go backwards with a wage than stand still without one. I'd swallow it.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to slow it down or pay people while it settles. I'd sign petitions online, though I'm not a protest person.
S2.think: I'd lose my job inside two years and Tomas would too, maybe sooner. I left the warehouse thinking I'd found something robots couldn't do, and now it's happening again.
S2.do: Cuts all unneeded spending and puts savings into paying down the mortgage, which has about six years left. Takes in a lodger in the back bedroom, and looks for any job still going, even back in a warehouse.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, because it would be the second time.
S2.quote: I'd rather go backwards with a wage than stand still without one.
S2.fieldNote: The sense of history repeating is what drives her alarm, not just the money. With two exposed jobs in the house, the savings feel thinner than they are. She's practical about taking a step back to keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still both of us, but with some room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and companies should have to give proper notice and training. I'd say it at work. I'd tell my younger cousin not to bother starting an apprenticeship in roofing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got time to do what I did at the warehouse, leave before it gets to me. The trouble is, leave for what? Last time there was construction. This time I don't know what the next thing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training first, because it still pays. Then by year two, once it's clear which jobs are holding up, I'd retrain into whatever that is, maybe looking after the machines on site or something in care. We'd keep overpaying the house, and Tomas and I would put off having kids for a few more years until we knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lying awake every night, but most Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care. Why care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's a care assistant. She says people still want a person to hold their hand, even if a machine lifts them. I don't know if that's true when the machines get that good, but it's the only thing I can think of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off having kids. Is that a big change for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. We'd talked about trying in a year or two. I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house where neither of us knows if we'll have work, so we'd wait. Tomas would agree, I think, but he'd be sad about it.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and companies should give proper notice and training. I'd tell my younger cousin not to start a roofing apprenticeship.
S3.think: I'd want to leave before it gets to me, like I did at the warehouse. The trouble is, last time there was construction to go to, and this time I don't know what the next thing is.
S3.do: Finishes her training first because it still pays, then by year two retrains into whatever is holding up, perhaps machine care on site or care work. Keeps overpaying the house and puts off having children for a few years.
S3.feel: Anxious, mostly on Sundays rather than every night.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house where neither of us knows if we'll have work, so we'd wait.
S3.fieldNote: She plans to repeat her warehouse move but can't name a destination this time. Care work comes from her mum's view, and she doubts it herself. The decision to delay children is the clearest cost of the five-year clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a real amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, so there's no excuse for governments or companies not to. I'd say we should start training people now. I'd say it sensibly, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think this one is manageable. I'd get a good few years on the roofs, pay off the house and then move into something else when I can see it working for other people. It's how I like to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training and work the roofs for maybe five years, paying off the house by then. I'd start using the AI tools more for planning and quotes, and around year five I'd retrain into whatever looks solid. And we'd go ahead with trying for a baby in the next year or two, like we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry in the background, but I could live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, you'd go ahead with a baby. With five, you'd wait. What's the difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten, the child would be in school before it hits, and the house would be ours. With five, I'd be pregnant or with a toddler right when everything goes. It's just timing, really, like everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe. He's fifty-two and he's the best roofer I've ever seen. In ten years he'd be sixty-two and the thing he's best at in the world wouldn't be needed. I think that would break his heart more than his bank account.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, so there's no excuse for governments or companies not to. We should start training people now.
S4.think: This one is manageable: a few years on the roofs, pay off the house, then move into something else once I see it working for others. That's how I like to do things.
S4.do: Finishes training and works roofs for about five years, paying off the house. Uses AI tools more for planning and quotes and retrains around year five into whatever looks solid, while going ahead with trying for a baby in the next year or two.
S4.feel: Uneasy, a background worry she can live with.
S4.quote: I think that would break his heart more than his bank account.
S4.fieldNote: Her family plans flip with the warning time, which she explains clearly as a matter of timing. Ten years fits her preferred way of moving once others have proved a path. Her concern for Joe is about pride and identity rather than money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Tomas and I would go at once and it'd be the warehouse all over again, with nowhere to jump to. What would help is proper notice, a year at least, and the government paying for retraining while you still get some wage. Last time I just had to work it out on my own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask people if they've been through it before. I have. It changes how you hear all of this. Once you've watched the robots come up one aisle at a time, you don't laugh at the videos anymore.

headlineQuote: Once you've watched the robots come up one aisle at a time, you don't laugh at the videos anymore.
portrait: Vera Rossi is a 27-year-old junior on a roofing and framing crew on a new housing estate, who came into construction after picking robots took over the warehouse where she used to work. She shares a small house with Tomas, a bus driver, mostly paid for with money her dad left, and has about eight months of savings. Pragmatic and steady, she moves once change is proven but tries to leave before it reaches her. She's calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady picture and alarmed by AGI in two years, when both their jobs would go at once. Longer timelines let her plan to pay off the house and retrain, and decide whether to have a child.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Tomas would both lose work at once and it would be the warehouse all over again with nowhere to jump to.
whatWouldHelp: At least a year's notice and government-paid retraining with some wage while it happens, so she isn't left to work it out alone again.
